nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
SUNDAY. 11:47 P.M.

Police lights turn the Marquee’s gold lettering blue. Eli’s camera lies on the wet lobby floor, still recording. A dark red smear marks Noah’s shirt. Someone pounds twice on the locked projection-booth door, then goes quiet.

“Whatever you do,” Eli says, watching the camera, “don’t play the last minute.”

Noah holds out his hand. “Maya. The key.”

I have no memory of picking it up.

FIVE DAYS EARLIER…

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
TUESDAY. 6:14 P.M.

The Marquee smells of dust, buttered popcorn and the worst coffee in Asheville. I’ve come back to design its reopening campaign, not to tell Noah Bennett I was fired in Atlanta. And certainly not to tell him about Monday’s Chicago interview.

Noah is holding the ladder we used to climb as teenagers. He remembers which rung wobbles. Of course he does.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
A stranger lowers a camera at the ticket counter. Dark curls. An inconveniently good smile.

“Eli Rivera. I’m filming the reopening. May I get the first poster going up?”

Noah takes the heavy poster tube from my hands without asking. “Careful. She bills extra for being charming.”

“You still owe me for 2019,” I say. Both men smile, but for different reasons.

choices.text: Let Eli film the poster—on my terms.
Keep the cameras off. Hang it with Noah.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
“Poster, not portrait,” I say. Eli swings the monitor toward me so I can check. No tricks.

Noah steadies the ladder while I work. My sleeve brushes his wrist; neither of us moves immediately. From behind the camera, Eli says, almost too softly, “You two have history.”

“We have a ladder,” I say. “It’s a long story.”

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Eli switches off the camera at once. “I’ll give the popcorn machine its close-up.”

Noah braces the ladder and hums the terrible tune we used to sing while closing. When I glance down, he’s already watching me.

For one dangerous second I remember the night we nearly kissed on the roof. He remembers too; I can tell by the way he changes the subject.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
THURSDAY. TWO DAYS LATER.

Eli shows me a rough cut. It’s gorgeous: the gold bulbs, Noah’s hands repairing a seat, my poster filling the screen. Then I see the file name on his laptop: FAREWELL_CUT_03.

“This is a reopening,” I say.

“It’s supposed to be.” He closes the laptop carefully. Across the lobby, Noah is arguing on the phone about a Monday collection. He stops when he sees me looking.

choices.text: Ask Eli who commissioned a farewell film.
Ask Eli for one honest conversation, without a camera.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
THURSDAY. TWO DAYS LATER.

Noah hands me coffee made exactly the way I take it. He also hides a bright orange tag under the projector-case handle.

MONDAY COLLECTION, it reads. Underneath, in smaller type: $4,000.

“So,” I say, “are we reopening a cinema or selling one?”

He doesn't make a joke. That worries me more than the tag.

choices.text: Give Noah room—but tell him secrecy has a deadline.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli doesn’t pretend he misunderstood. His producer is funded by a group hoping to redevelop the block. They paid him to document the Marquee’s “final days.”

“I pushed back,” he says. “I thought if the place survived, I’d have a better film.”

“And you never thought I should know?”

His silence is an answer. Noah has heard enough from the doorway. “You pointed a camera at us for people who want this place gone?”

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli puts the camera away. He tells me he has a contract he regrets signing and a producer who wants a particular ending. He doesn’t say whose money is behind it.

“Then you can start by showing me the entire cut,” I say.

“You’ll get it tomorrow.”

We sit together in the darkened auditorium. His shoulder is close, but he leaves the distance for me to cross—or not.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Noah rubs his eyes. “I took a refundable deposit against the old projector. Four thousand. It paid the staff what I owed them.”

“And if you can't repay it?”

“They take the projector Monday.”

He looks at the poster I designed: ONE MORE FIRST NIGHT.

“I should have told you before you promised people something I might not deliver.” His honesty arrives late enough to hurt.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
“By Saturday, you’ll have the whole picture,” Noah says. “If you hate me then, at least you’ll have the facts.”

“That's not particularly comforting.”

“I was aiming for mysterious.”

He reaches for my hand, then stops short. The restraint is somehow worse. When I leave, I see him fold the orange tag into his pocket like a letter he cannot bear to open.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
SATURDAY. THE NIGHT BEFORE REOPENING.

Noah wants to confront Eli’s producer in public. Eli wants to show me his objection email and let me decide whether the film screens. Both are asking me to trust them after keeping something from me.

My phone glows: CHICAGO INTERVIEW — MONDAY. A future neither of them gets to decide for me.

I can feel the old pull toward Noah, the new one toward Eli—and the possibility of choosing neither tonight.

choices.text: Stand beside Noah, but refuse a public ambush.
Hear Eli out—but demand control of my image.
Take charge of the screening plan myself.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
SATURDAY. THE NIGHT BEFORE REOPENING.

Eli sends the rough cut. It stops abruptly just before Noah opens the projection booth. In the last frame, the door is marked with a fresh scrape.

Noah finds me staring at it. “You could have asked me,” he says.

“I did ask someone. He gave me a beautiful half-answer.”

Tomorrow, people will see whichever story we let onto that screen.

choices.text: Show Noah the missing minute and ask for the truth.
Ask Eli to show me the unedited footage.
Keep the clip private and make my own plan.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
SATURDAY. THE NIGHT BEFORE REOPENING.

Noah’s confession sits between us, heavier than the projector. The employees were paid; the cinema could still lose its heart on Monday.

Eli’s camera is on the ticket counter, switched off. “Whatever you decide,” he says, “let it be your decision.”

My Chicago reminder flashes again. I have been hiding a future of my own. No one in this room is entirely innocent of silence.

choices.text: Help Noah tell the staff the truth, together.
Ask Eli to document the facts, not a tragedy.
Rework the campaign without promising a miracle.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
SATURDAY. THE NIGHT BEFORE REOPENING.

Noah finally says, “I may lose the projector Monday.” He doesn't say why. Eli sets his camera facedown when I enter. In one room: two men trying to make me feel safe by deciding what I shouldn't know.

My interview reminder lights up. Funny how much secrecy can fit into a small cinema.

Noah takes a step toward me. Eli waits at the far end of the aisle. I get to decide where I stand.

choices.text: Tell Noah I care, but I need the whole truth.
Walk with Eli and ask what he isn't saying.
Leave them both waiting. Finish my own work.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Noah lets his anger settle before he speaks. “I wanted to save this place. I forgot other people get to decide how.” He agrees to face Eli without humiliating him.

In the projection booth, he shows me an empty hook where the brass key should hang. “It was here an hour ago.”

When he reaches for my hand, I take it. For now. Somewhere downstairs, a door closes too sharply.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli forwards the objection email, dated before he met me. It changes what I think of him; it doesn't erase the lie. I insist on reviewing every frame containing me.

“I’m not asking you to forgive me,” he says. “I’m asking you to hold me to something better.”

His phone vibrates: PRODUCER — YOU HAVE UNTIL SUNDAY. He turns the screen toward me this time.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
I replace SAVE THE MARQUEE with COME SEE WHAT WE’RE FIGHTING FOR. No promise about money. No sentimental lie.

Noah agrees to give the audience the real numbers. Eli agrees not to screen the film without consent. Their relief almost makes me smile.

Then a message arrives from an unknown number: ASK THEM WHAT HAPPENED IN THE BOOTH. Attached is one blurry photograph.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Noah watches the last frame, jaw tight. “The booth door has been sticking since Tuesday,” he says. “Someone should have fixed it.”

“Is that the whole story?” I ask.

“No.” He holds my gaze. “And I owe you more than a goodnight kiss to distract you.”

I hadn't offered a kiss. I might have, before he said that. He gives me the key to the booth and asks me to meet him in the morning.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli sends the raw footage instead of another explanation. The final minute shows a man carrying a heavy case out of the booth—but his face is outside the frame.

“That isn't in the producer's edit,” Eli says. “They wanted a simpler villain.”

For the first time, he looks frightened of his own camera. I ask him to keep a copy where neither of us can quietly delete it.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
I make two copies of the rough cut and write down exactly what it does—and doesn't—show. I have spent too many years letting confident men narrate uncertainty.

At midnight I print fresh posters. When the printer stops, someone slips an envelope under the cinema office door. Inside: a brass key and a note. DO NOT TRUST THE FINAL CUT.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
We call the senior staff member together. Noah doesn't excuse taking the deposit; he explains why he did it and what losing the projector would mean. The silence afterward is painful, but honest.

On the way back, he says, “I used to think you were the brave one.”

“I'm still deciding.”

He almost kisses me by the stairwell. An unfamiliar knock from the locked projection booth interrupts us.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
I give Eli the deposit receipt and the workers' side of the story. “If you use this,” I say, “you show both.”

He studies me instead of the document. “You're better at protecting people than I am.”

“Try harder. It's cheaper than apologies.”

His producer calls; he lets it ring. When it stops, a new message appears: DELIVER THE FAREWELL CUT OR LOSE THE DEAL.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
My new campaign promises a screening, a conversation, and the truth about the Marquee's finances. Not salvation. I text my Chicago interviewer to confirm Monday's time.

Noah thanks me without asking me to stay. Eli offers to design the title card and accepts my no.

Then the cinema lights flicker. In the booth, a metal case has been moved, leaving four bright scratches across the floor.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
“The projector is pledged as collateral,” Noah finally says. “I used the money to pay the staff.”

“Thank you for telling me,” I say. “I wish you'd trusted me earlier.”

He puts the brass booth key between us, like an offering. “You don't owe me a rescue.”

It is the closest thing to a love confession he's ever made. I leave the key on the counter. Neither of us touches it.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Outside, Eli admits his producer expects a farewell film, not a comeback. “They didn't hire me to find out what happens,” he says. “They hired me to confirm what they'd already decided.”

“And what do you want?”

He smiles without enjoying it. “Until tonight I thought I knew.”

He offers me the uncut footage. I ask him to send it before we talk about anything else.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
I finish my posters alone. The last line reads: ONE MORE FIRST NIGHT. WHAT COMES AFTER IS OURS TO DECIDE.

Chicago still has my interview on Monday. Asheville still has the two men I refuse to become a prize for. Both things can be true.

As I lock up, I hear two knocks from upstairs. The projection-booth light is on, although I switched it off an hour ago.
